title: Tracking Issue: Adoption of CPython limited API

labels.name: 63 - C API
labels.description: Changes or additions to the C API. Mailing list should usually be notified.

body:
**Description:**

As discussed with @mattip, this issue tracks the long term effort of moving NumPy to the CPython [limited API](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/stable.html).

With CPython moving toward subinterpreters, free-threading, and forward-compatible wheels, adopting the limited API will give us more flexibility. This will be a gradual process, and the immediate goal is just to tackle the low-hanging fruit. 

**Important:** This work must be entirely internal. It should not change performance, usability, or NumPy's own C-API.

#### Roadmap:

- Migrate the codebase on a module-by-module basis by replacing restricted C-API calls with `Py_LIMITED_API` alternatives and updating the build configuration to compile those newly compliant files with the `Py_LIMITED_API` macro.

#### Expected Outcomes for this phase:

* Updating C files so many of them can define the `Py_LIMITED_API` macro and still compile.
* Forward-compatible abi3 wheels.

- What problem does this PR solve?
  Fixes #17463.   It makes sequence splitting consistent across the entire family of split functions and prevents unexpected runtime `AttributeError` crashes for downstream code passing lists or tuples.

title: BUG: set_typeDict() accepts non-dict objects and causes SystemError in later promote_types()
body:
### Describe the issue:

`numpy._core._multiarray_umath.set_typeDict()` accepts arbitrary Python objects and stores them as the internal `typeDict` state without checking that the object is a dictionary.

A later call to `promote_types()` can then pass this invalid object to a CPython dictionary API, resulting in:

```text
SystemError: Objects/dictobject.c:1760: bad argument to internal function
```

The relevant code in `numpy/_core/src/multiarray/descriptor.c` currently does:

```c
if (!PyArg_ParseTuple(args, "O:set_typeDict", &dict)) {
    return NULL;
}
multiarray_umath_state *state = get_module_state(module);
Py_XSETREF(state->typeDict, Py_NewRef(dict));
```

There is no validation that `dict` is actually a dictionary before it is stored in `state->typeDict`.

The later dtype handling path uses this value as a dictionary, which is what leads to the internal `SystemError`.

I believe the invalid value should be rejected by `set_typeDict()` before it replaces the existing internal dictionary.

### Reproduce the code example:

```python
import numpy as np

m = np._core._multiarray_umath

# Install an invalid object into the internal typeDict state.
m.set_typeDict(object())

# This later consumes typeDict through the dictionary API.
m.promote_types(
    r"p.fJ*PkER\d.E*\Z.\Z+Y\ZS\SEJtYUyN*.PUvfaca.q",
    r"kdyZgb.YOGTK.k\dc.zDVBOx\B.+.qY*C..\B\sp\wvd.",
)
```

### Error message:

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
SystemError: Objects/dictobject.c:1760: bad argument to internal function
```

### Python and NumPy Versions:

```text
NumPy: 2.6.0.dev0+git20260925.a98529d
Python: 3.12.14
Python implementation: CPython
Platform: Linux x86_64 (WSL2)
Compiler: GCC 13.3.0
NumPy build: debug build with optimizations disabled
NumPy commit: a98529dfd92d73fd4d40ebaaf285cf2463bb92b1
```

### Runtime Environment:

Linux x86_64 under WSL2.

The NumPy build was configured as a debug build with optimizations disabled and was built locally from the NumPy development tree.

Python:

```text
3.12.14
```

Compiler:

```text
GCC 13.3.0
```

### How does this issue affect you or how did you find it:

I found this while running Fusil against NumPy's native `_multiarray_umath` module.

The original Fusil-generated testcase exercised a number of native functions. The failure was initially reported at `promote_types()`. I then reduced the testcase and found that `set_typeDict()` was the important state-changing operation before the failure.

The relevant sequence is:

```text
set_typeDict(non-dict)
        |
        v
invalid object stored in typeDict
        |
        v
promote_types(...)
        |
        v
CPython dictionary API
        |
        v
SystemError
```

The failure is deterministic with the preserved Fusil-generated testcase.

I also tested the same testcase after adding a dictionary check to `set_typeDict()`:

```c
if (!PyDict_Check(dict)) {
    PyErr_SetString(PyExc_TypeError,
            "set_typeDict() argument must be a dictionary");
    return NULL;
}
```

With this validation in place, the same testcase no longer produces the `SystemError`.

Instead, `set_typeDict()` raises:

```text
TypeError: set_typeDict() argument must be a dictionary
```

and the later `promote_types()` call produces a normal dtype-related `TypeError` instead of the CPython internal `SystemError`.

So the issue appears to be that `set_typeDict()` can leave the internal `typeDict` state containing an object that is not a dictionary, which is only detected later when another native operation uses it as a dictionary.

### How it was found

Found while fuzzing NumPy's native `_multiarray_umath` module with [Fusil](https://github.com/devdanzin/fusil). The generated testcase was minimized to `set_typeDict(non-dict)` followed by `promote_types()`, reproducing the `SystemError` independently of Fusil.

title: BUG: preserve BitGenerator state after failed reinitialization
body:
### PR summary

Closes #28784

This PR fixes a segmentation fault that can occur when an existing NumPy random `BitGenerator` is reinitialized with invalid input and the reinitialization fails.

Previously, `BitGenerator.__init__()` could reset parts of the existing instance before the new seed had been fully validated. As a result, a failed reinitialization could raise the expected Python exception while still leaving the existing `BitGenerator` with an invalid internal state. A subsequent call to `random_raw()` could then dereference that invalid state and crash the interpreter.

This PR changes initialization so that seed validation is completed before the existing `BitGenerator` state is mutated. If reinitialization fails, the exception is raised while the previously valid generator state is preserved.

`Philox` requires additional handling because its `counter` and `key` arguments are validated separately from the base seed. Their conversion and validation are therefore also performed before calling `BitGenerator.__init__()`, preventing an invalid `counter` or `key` from partially reinitializing an existing Philox instance.

Regression tests verify that failed reinitialization preserves the previous random stream for:

* `MT19937`
* `PCG64`
* `PCG64DXSM`
* `SFC64`
* `Philox`

Additional tests cover failed Philox reinitialization with invalid `counter` and `key` values.

**Before the fix:**

```python
>>> import numpy.random
>>> p = numpy.random.PCG64DXSM()
>>> try:
...     p.__init__(("",))
... except ValueError:
...     pass
...
>>> p.random_raw()
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
```

**After the fix:**

```python
>>> import numpy.random
>>> p = numpy.random.PCG64DXSM(123)
>>> try:
...     p.__init__(("",))
... except ValueError:
...     pass
...
>>> p.random_raw()
# Returns normally using the previously valid generator state.
```

Standard successful initialization behavior is unchanged. The additional validation occurs during initialization/reinitialization and does not add checks to the random-number generation hot path.

### First time contributor introduction

This is my first contribution to NumPy. I have previously contributed to SciPy and Python-Blosc2, and I am interested in continuing to contribute to the Scientific Python ecosystem.

### AI Disclosure
Tool used: Anthropic's Claude Code
I used AI-assisted tooling to investigate and draft this fix; I've reviewed, tested, and can explain every change above.

title: Build release notes from MyST Markdown
body:
This is a proof-of-concept PR to show how markdown release notes would look using the `myst_parser` plugin for Sphinx. There are **two commits**, which I recommend we look at separately: [the first](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/32768/commits/9fd7df70ad874acb60d4f26ea0cc30961bca26b8) is for updating the Sphinx machinery (that one we can cherry-pick in the future), and [the second](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/32768/commits/b845fff5acf739959ee07aab4cdb22745f01c597) to show the syntax changes to the release note snippets themselves (we wouldn't merge this, since we can simply switch to the new machinery after a next release).

`myst_parser` is pretty forgiving, in the sense that if a role is not used by `myst`, it passes it through as a Sphinx directive. That's why so few changes are needed to the notes, and why maintainers won't need to memorize a new syntax. If, in some future, we switch over to https://mystmd.org, the changes will be more extensive, since that engine *only* supports myst markdown.

I made this PR after a discussion on the community call, to better inform a decision; it is simply a demonstration, and there is no NEED to switch now.

See https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/23805 for background.

title: ENH: support `where=` in MaskedArray reductions
body:
### Proposed new feature or change: ndarray reductions accept a where= keyword to select which elements participate in the reduction. The corresponding MaskedArray methods don't — they raise TypeError, even though they do support keepdims. 
 
import numpy as np, numpy.ma as ma

x = ma.array([1, 2, 3, 4], mask=[0, 1, 0, 0])

# ndarray: works
np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]).sum(where=[True, True, False, False])  # -> 3

# MaskedArray: TypeError
x.sum(where=[True, True, False, False])
# TypeError: MaskedArray.sum() got an unexpected keyword argument 'where'
Note that the top-level np.sum(x, where=...) also raises, since it dispatches to x.sum(where=...) via _wrapreduction. So there is no working way to pass where= on a MaskedArray through the standard API today. Affected methods on MaskedArray: sum, prod, mean, var, std, min, max, any, all Workaround today Users can combine the mask and where manually and reduce on the raw data: 
where_condition = np.array([True, True, False, False])
combined = ~np.ma.getmaskarray(x) & where_condition   # elements that are unmasked AND selected
result = np.sum(x.data, where=combined)      # -> 1
This works, but it reaches into x.data and x.mask, bypassing the MaskedArray abstraction. It also requires getmaskarray because x.mask is the singleton nomask when nothing is masked; ~x.mask fails in that case. And it doesn't compose cleanly with methods like mean or min, where the reduction semantics also depend on how masked elements are handled. Native where= support on MaskedArray reductions would let users write x.sum(where=...) directly, with the mask combined internally. Question 1- Is the missing where= intentional on MaskedArray or an oversight? 2- The natural semantic seems to be where combined with the existing mask — an element participates only if it is both unmasked and selected by where. Please advise if there is interest, and I'd be happy to open a PR.

title: DEP: Deprecate np.dot when second argument has >2 dimensions

labels.name: sustain-2026
labels.description: Issues reserved for NumFOCUS Sustaining Open Source Series 2026

body:
Closes #31725

### PR summary

**What problem does this PR solve?**

`np.dot()` and `ndarray.dot()` have a dimension-interleaving behavior when the second argument has more than 2 dimensions. For example:

```python
a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((4, 3, 5))
np.dot(a, b).shape  # (2, 4, 5) - the 4 ends up in the middle
```

Most users expect either `(2, 5)` (like regular matrix multiplication) or `(4, 2, 5)` (batch dimension at front, like `@`/`matmul`). The interleaved result `(2, 4, 5)` is surprising and rarely intended.

**Ecosystem research:** We checked 9 downstream libraries (scipy, scikit-learn, astropy, pandas, xarray, matplotlib, statsmodels, seaborn, networkx) and found no usage of `np.dot` with a >2D second argument outside of test files. Details posted in #31725.

This PR adds a deprecation warning when the second argument has >2 dimensions, suggesting `numpy.tensordot(a, b, axes=[-1, -2])` for the same result or `@`/`matmul` for standard batched operations.

**Changes:**
- Created internal `PyArray_MatrixProduct_int()` with `warn_on_interleave` flag, following NumPy's `_int` suffix convention
- All public functions call it directly: `PyArray_MatrixProduct`, `PyArray_MatrixProduct2`, `array_matrixproduct` (np.dot), `array_dot` (ndarray.dot)
- `np.inner` and C extensions call via the public API with `warn=0`
- Warning fires only when `a.ndim >= 2` AND `b.ndim > 2` (actual dimension interleaving)
- Deprecation check runs after shape validation, so shape mismatch raises `ValueError` (not `DeprecationWarning`) even with `-W error`. Also, reusing existing cleanup paths (no redundant conversions).
- Updated `np.dot` docstring with `.. deprecated:: 2.6` note
- Added `TestDotDimensionInterleaving` class in `test_deprecations.py` with 7 tests (including shape mismatch priority test)
- Docstring examples use `# doctest: +SKIP` so users see the DeprecationWarning when running the code
- Updated masked array tests in `test_core.py` and `test_extras.py`
- Added release note (`32759.deprecation.rst`)

**Why an internal wrapper?**

The deprecation check was initially placed in `PyArray_MatrixProduct2()`, but `np.inner()` also calls this shared function and should not trigger the warning. Rather than duplicating the matrix product logic, we created an internal implementation with a flag parameter. This avoids code duplication while keeping the warning scoped to `np.dot`/`ndarray.dot` only.

**Lesson learned:** Running `spin test` (the full test suite) locally before pushing catches failures earlier, rather than discovering them in CI. Additionally, running the doctest suite (`spin test -- --doctest-modules --doctest-only-doctests=true --doctest-collect=api`) catches failures in docstring examples that unit tests miss.

#### AI Disclosure

AI assisted with codebase navigation, identifying NumPy conventions for deprecation warnings and tests, and drafting code and documentation. All changes were reviewed and tested locally before submitting.

title: ENH: Improve MT19937 uint{32,64} workloads
body:
This patch introduces three new methods to the interface of the BitGenerator class with the intent of speeding up the generation of uint32 and uint64 values when using the MT19937 method.This patch leaves the other generators untouched.

The new methods deliver speedups because the new c implementation makes it easier for the compiler to inline and optimize the MT19937 generation algorithm which currently, in the per element loop, relies on virtual calls to the appropriate BitGenerator methods. In case the new interface methods are available in the selected generator, then for bounded generation I have also implemented the Lemire procedure to ensure that the output values are in the expected range.

On a Graviton 4 machine, the following speedups, defined as time with native numpy over the patched code, were observed for the benchmarks that I think are relevant to these changes: numpy/bench_random.RNG and numpy/bench_random.Bounded. In particular:

   |  uint16 | 1535     |   1.0x                                              |

 -Wl,--gc-sections -o mt19937`

were the following:

title: BUG: Fix np.trim_zeros TypeError for multi-dimensional lists/tuples
body:
Fixes #32394

 was raising `TypeError` for multi-dimensional Python sequences (lists of lists, tuples of tuples) because tuple-style slicing (`filt[sl]` where `sl` is a tuple of slices) was applied directly to the original list/tuple, which doesn't support multi-dimensional indexing with tuples.

### Changes
- For multi-dimensional inputs (ndim > 1), slice the `np.asarray`-converted array instead of the original input
- Convert the result back to the original input type:
  - Lists: use `.tolist()`
  - Tuples: recursively convert nested arrays to tuples to preserve the nested tuple structure
- 1D case remains unchanged to preserve existing behavior (returns list/tuple as before)

### Test Plan

All cases now work without raising TypeError.

title: PERF: add a SIMD fast path for masked ufunc loops
body:
Closes #32136
### PR summary

Currently, masked ufunc loops walk runs of unmasked values. So the more often masked/unmasked values alternate, the slower it gets.

This PR fixes that. New strategy(`gather_masked_strided_loop` in `array_method_masked.dispatch.cpp`) for contiguous arrays of 2/4/8-byte numeric types:

The new loop processes fixed blocks of 128 elements and counts the unmasked ones.

- if 0: skip the block
- if 128: process the whole block
- if < 16 or > 112(= 128 - 16) : generic algorithm
- else: compress the inputs into a 128-element buffer, apply the operation to the compressed data, expand back into the output.

block size=128 stored in NPY_MASKED_GATHER_BLOCKSIZE.
count below which the algo uses generic path = 16 stored in NPY_MASKED_GATHER_WALK_LIMIT

The simd work is done with Highway in `array_method_masked.dispatch.cpp`. This is built through meson `multi_targets`, so x86 gets its AVX instead of SSE2 baseline. The target resolves once per Numpy initialization.

The tail (n % 128) falls back to the loop from `generic_masked_strided_loop`, which I factored out into the `generic_masked_strided_loop_helper` function.

title: BUG: ndarray.__reduce__ converts shape errors to SystemError
body:
### Describe the issue:

`ndarray.__reduce__()` does not propagate exceptions raised by a subclass's `shape` property.

In `array_reduce()`, the result of `PyObject_GetAttrString(self, "shape")` is passed directly to `PyTuple_SET_ITEM()` without checking for `NULL`. If the attribute access raises, `array_reduce()` can return a non-NULL result while an exception is still set, which results in `SystemError`.

This is reproducible with an `ndarray` subclass that overrides `shape`.

### Reproduce the code example:

```python
import numpy as np
import pickle


class BadArray(np.ndarray):
    @property
    def shape(self):
        raise RuntimeError("bad shape")


arr = np.array([1, 2, 3]).view(BadArray)

arr.__reduce__()
```

### Error message:

```shell
SystemError: <method '__reduce__' of 'numpy.ndarray' objects> returned a result with an exception set
```

### Python and NumPy Versions:

Python 3.12.6
NumPy 2.6.0.dev0+git20260925.b40d1b4

### Runtime Environment:

Windows 64-bit

### How does this issue affect you or how did you find it:

This was found while triaging a C-extension audit reported in this gist:
https://gist.github.com/devdanzin/ccc2d9553ca1c90ab1835362ee21a40a8

After checking the finding against current main, I reproduced it with an ndarray subclass overriding shape. A local null check for the shape lookup makes the original RuntimeError propagate correctly through both __reduce__() and pickle.dumps().

I'm opening this issue first to confirm the expected behavior before preparing a fix.

title: TYP: Fix np.gradient return type when axis is passed

labels.name: 09 - Backport-Candidate
labels.description: PRs tagged should be backported

body:
### PR summary
Closes #32770

Adds overloads to handle the specific scalar (or 1D tuple) `axes` case I identified in #32770 (from one of my own repos), plus enumerating all the cases where a 2, or 3D tuple could be specified as an argument for `axes`, with a fallback if it is not recognized. These cases actually return Tuples of the same dimensionality as axes, instead of the `_Mesh2D`/`_Mesh3D`  case that they were previously declared to return, so this will fix other several latent cases where the return type would have been declared incorrectly. 

In the case where `axes` is specified differently, e.g. a list instead of a tuple, there is an explicit overload for an `Any` fallback, rather than guessing. That fallback may result in a few downstream cases where typing is broadened, but that may be unavoidable, to avoid an _incorrect_ type in an edge case.

Because the axes argument is now fully handled with their own overloads, all of the other existing overloads (except the ones that actually do return a `_Mesh` like object) now only take `None` for `axes`.

**Limitation**
This could easily be extended to handle 4D cases, which some of the other functions in this file do, but `gradient` doesn't have any 4D overloads right now so I didn't add them.

### First time contributor introduction
I am an astrophysics postdoctoral researcher who uses numpy for a variety of numerical python codes (e.g., almost everything I do). I am steadily trying to type all my python codes, and  ran into this error. I have previously contributed to other open sources projects like e.g. numba and scipy and opened another numpy issue in the past, but haven't contributed a PR to numpy directly before. 


#### AI Disclosure
The cause of the `pyright` error I was experiencing was originally diagnosed as a type stub issue by Claude Opus 5.5. I drafted the fix with the assistance of Codex GPT-6.0 Astra to help enumerate all the edge cases. I cross-reviewed the fix for consistency with local conventions with Claude Fable 5.1, which had no findings. I wrote the issue text, commit message, and entire PR body myself with no AI assistance.

This commit adds another build option, `cpu-dispatch-default`, which can be used
to enable a subset of the dispatched CPU features by default.

If `cpu-dispatch-default` is not set (or == 'none') there is no behavior change:
1. if neither `NPY_DISABLE_CPU_FEATURES` nor `NPY_ENABLE_CPU_FEATURES` is specified we enable the maximal features
2. if `NPY_DISABLE_CPU_FEATURES` is specified we still use the maximum, but disable the requested features
3. if `NPY_ENABLE_CPU_FEATURES` is specified we enable nothing but the requested features
```

(numpy_dev_venv) bessen@bessen-rh8.toa(nyc):/codemill/bessen/opensource/numpy (cpu_dispatch_default)$ NPY_DISABLE_CPU_FEATURES="AVX2" python3 -c 'from numpy._core._multiarray_umath import __cpu_features__ as f, __cpu_dispatch__ as d; print({n: f[n] for n in d})'
{'SSSE3': True, 'SSE41': True, 'POPCNT': True, 'SSE42': True, 'AVX': True, 'F16C': True, 'FMA3': True, 'AVX2': False, 'AVX512F': True, 'AVX512CD': True, 'AVX512_KNL': False, 'AVX512_KNM': False, 'AVX512_SKX': True, 'AVX512_CLX': True, 'AVX512_CNL': False, 'AVX512_ICL': False}
(numpy_dev_venv) bessen@bessen-rh8.toa(nyc):/codemill/bessen/opensource/numpy (cpu_dispatch_default)$ NPY_ENABLE_CPU_FEATURES="AVX512F" python3 -c 'from numpy._core._multiarray_umath import __cpu_features__ as f, __cpu_dispatch__ as d; print({n: f[n] for n in d})'
{'SSSE3': False, 'SSE41': False, 'POPCNT': False, 'SSE42': False, 'AVX': False, 'F16C': False, 'FMA3': False, 'AVX2': False, 'AVX512F': True, 'AVX512CD': False, 'AVX512_KNL': False, 'AVX512_KNM': False, 'AVX512_SKX': False, 'AVX512_CLX': False, 'AVX512_CNL': False, 'AVX512_ICL': False}
```

However, if `cpu-dispatch-default` is set at compilation time then those features
are enabled by default if supported by the CPU:
1. if neither `NPY_DISABLE_CPU_FEATURES` nor `NPY_ENABLE_CPU_FEATURES` is specified we enable the (supported) default features
2. if `NPY_DISABLE_CPU_FEATURES` is specified we start from the (supported) default features and disable the requested features
3. if `NPY_ENABLE_CPU_FEATURES` is specified we enable those features in addition to the (supported) default features

As an example, consider `cpu-dispatch-default='avx2 fma3'`:
```
(numpy_dev_venv) bessen@bessen-rh8.toa(nyc):/codemill/bessen/opensource/numpy (cpu_dispatch_default)$ python3 -c 'from numpy._core._multiarray_umath import __cpu_features__ as f, __cpu_dispatch__ as d; print({n: f[n] for n in d})'
```

body:
This fixes two typing issues in `np.array`:

- Depending on the type-checker, passing a nested list literal to `np.array` lead to incorrect or unintentionally broad result types. This smells like a bug (plural actually) to me, because those overloads are disjoint, so order should not have mattered. I've added a note about this in the stubs.

title: TYP: prevent ``Literal`` shape-type propagation in array constructors
body:
Depending on the type-checker, array constructors like `np.ones((2, 3))` would be inferred as `ndarray[tuple[Literal[2], Literal[3]], ...]` instead of the desired `ndarray[tuple[int, int], ...]`. This replaces the `ShapeT: tuple[int, ....]` with a "typevar with constraints" (for the lack of a better name) of explicitly upcasted shape-types.
The downside of this approach is that now only <=4d ranks are propagated, and >4d ones are now caught by the fallback overloads and will be inferred as `tuple[Any, ...]` (which is backwards compatible). I'm afraid there's no better solution though.

For completeness' sake, these functions are affected:

- `empty`
- `zeros`
- `ones`
- `full`
- `reshape`
- `broadcast_to`
- `random.Generator.*` (those with a `size=` param)

title: TYP: Improve support for unbounded tuples of `None` in array scalar `__getitem__()`
body:
### PR summary

#### Updated summary

On current `main` there are `generic.__getitem__()` and `void.__getitem__()` overloads for tuples of `None` with all possible lengths. But because the Python typing specification does not require type checkers to expand unbounded tuples then the annotations can be expected to work only with tuples the lengths of which are known statically. In practice arguments with the type `tuple[None, ...]` cause [type checking errors](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/32763#issuecomment-5800603791) with mypy, pyrefly and ty. This PR updates the overloads so that unbounded tuples of `None` can be type checked too.

#### Original summary

There already are tests for array scalar `__getitem__()` annotations using tuples of `None` with statically known lengths. The first commit here adds tests for variadic `None` tuples, which reveal that at least mypy has trouble in such cases. The second commit updates annotations of `generic.__getitem__()` and `void.__getitem__()` so that variadic `None` tuples can be type checked well enough (with mypy).~

I suspect variadic `None` tuples might be relevant in cases that look something like
```
def f(..., shape: Shape, ...):
    ...
    some_ufunc(...)[shape]
    ...
```
where `Shape` might be a type union containing `tuple[None, ...]`. Most importantly, the updated annotations make it clear that if the `some_ufunc()` call can return an array scalar and `shape` can be an empty tuple then `some_ufunc(...)[shape]` is not guaranteed to be an array but can be an array scalar instead.

### PR summary
Discovered as a problem for https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/32577.

In order for `np.minmax` to be used as a replacement for `np.min(...), np.max(...)` , it needs to work similarly for all cases. The problem was that user dtypes like rational and bfloat16 promoted. title: BUG: numpy logarithm behavior does not match CPython 3.14 `cmath.log` behavior
body:
### Describe the issue:

In CPython 3.14, the behavior of logarithms of complex numbers changed for some edge case inputs in https://github.com/python/cpython/commit/2cb84b107ad136eafb6e3d69145b7bdaefcca879, causing behavior to differ beyond floating point precision differences between

```python
import cmath

cmath.log(x, base)
```

and

```python
import numpy as np

np.log(x) / np.log(base)
```

where

```python
x = 1j
base = -cmath.inf + cmath.nanj
```

### Reproduce the code example:

```python
import cmath
import numpy as np
import warnings


def python(x, base):
    return cmath.log(x, base)


def numpy(x, base):
    return np.log(x) / np.log(base)


def numpy_scimath(x, base):
    return np.emath.logn(base, x)


def main():
    x = 1j
    base = -cmath.inf + cmath.nanj
    funcs = python, numpy, numpy_scimath
    names = list(map(lambda x: x.__name__, funcs))
    padding = max(map(len, names))

    for name, func in zip(names, funcs):
        print(f"{name}".ljust(padding) + ":", func(x, base))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)
        main()

```

In 3.13, this produces:

```
python       : (nan+nanj)
numpy        : (nan+nanj)
numpy_scimath: (nan+nanj)
```

In 3.14, this produces:

title: BUG: cast NaT to NaN when casting to float/complex
body:
### PR summary
Closes #26177

This PR changes the casting of `np.datetime64('NaT')` and `np.timedelta64('NaT')` to floating-point and complex types so that `NaT` is converted to `NaN`.

Internally, `NaT` is stored as the minimum `int64` value, so casting to a `float` type used that value as-is, producing `-9.2e18`. For `float16`, the value is out of range, so it became `-inf` along with an overflow warning.
With this change, `NaT` is now converted to `NaN` without any warning.

Before the fix (numpy 2.5.3):
```python
>>> np.array([np.datetime64('NaT', 's'), 1], dtype=object).astype(float)
array([-9.22337204e+18,  1.00000000e+00])
>>> np.array([np.timedelta64('NaT', 's'), 1+2j], dtype=object).astype(complex)
array([-9.22337204e+18+0.j,  1.00000000e+00+2.j])
>>> np.array(['NaT', '2024-01-01'], dtype='M8[D]').astype(float)
array([-9.22337204e+18,  1.97230000e+04])
>>> np.array(['NaT', 5], dtype='m8[s]').astype(np.float16)
<stdin>:1: RuntimeWarning: overflow encountered in cast
array([-inf,   5.], dtype=float16)
>>> np.float64(np.datetime64('NaT', 's'))
np.float64(-9.223372036854776e+18)
```

After the fix (local build of `main` with this patch applied):
```python
>>> np.array([np.datetime64('NaT', 's'), 1], dtype=object).astype(float)
array([nan,  1.])
>>> np.array([np.timedelta64('NaT', 's'), 1+2j], dtype=object).astype(complex)
array([nan+0.j,  1.+2.j])
>>> np.array(['NaT', '2024-01-01'], dtype='M8[D]').astype(float)
array([   nan, 19723.])
>>> np.array(['NaT', 5], dtype='m8[s]').astype(np.float16)
array([nan,  5.], dtype=float16)
>>> np.float64(np.datetime64('NaT', 's'))
np.float64(nan)
```

Casting to integer and bool types is unchanged.
Integer types have no equivalent of `NaN`, and with `int64` the `NaT` sentinel is preserved as the minimum value, so the existing behavior already round-trips back to `NaT` when cast back to a datetime type.
For bool, `NaT` evaluates to `True`, just like `NaN` does.

Same output before and after the fix:
```
>>> np.array(['NaT', 5], dtype='m8[s]').astype(np.int64)
array([-9223372036854775808,                    5])
>>> np.array(['NaT', 5], dtype='m8[s]').astype(bool)
array([ True,  True])
```

### First time contributor introduction

title: BUG: cast NaT to NaN when casting to float/complex
body:
NaT is stored as the minimum int64 value, and casts to floating-point types used that value as is, giving -9.2e18. For float16 the value is out of range, so the cast gave -inf along with an overflow warning.

The reverse cast already maps NaN to NaT. To match it, map NaT to NaN. For complex types, the real part is NaN and the imaginary part is 0.

Casts to integer types and bool are unchanged. Integer types have no equivalent of NaN, and for int64 NaT stays the minimum value, so casting back to datetime gives NaT again. For bool, NaT is true, the same as NaN.

Closes #26177

title: PERF: avoid temporary allocation in np.gradient for strided axes
body:
### PR summary

I investigated np.gradient and found out the central difference quotient was calculated in one line in _function_base_impl.py 

```python
out[slice1_t] = (f[slice4_t] - f[slice2_t]) / (2. * ax_dx) 
```

So first it calculates the difference f[slice4_t] - f[slice2_t], creates a temporary array for that result, then does the division by 2 * dx and saves the final result in out. This costs unnecessary memory and memory bandwidth, especially for large arrays. For some cases it is faster to calculate the difference, directly save the result in out and then scale out further.

## Explanation

For normal numpy arrays (C-order arrays), the last axis is contiguous in memory. For Fortran-order arrays (F-order arrays), the first axis is contiguous in memory. My tests showed that the existing method is good or sometimes even better for contiguous axes. But for non-contiguous, strided axes, the new proposed method is faster.
Therefore, I kept the existing method for contiguous axes and uses the new method as a case only for strided axes.

## Results
float32, C-order, (1000, 1000), axis=0:
196 µs -> 137 µs

float64, C-order, (1000, 1000), axis=0:
377 µs -> 273 µs

float32, F-order, (1000, 1000), axis=1:
196 µs -> 137 µs

float64, F-order, (1000, 1000), axis=1:
379 µs -> 270 µs

The added ASV benchmarks showed an increase of roughly 25-40% for the new method on strided-axis cases (tested on MacOS/arm64 , Apple M4 Max).

PERFORMANCE INCREASED."

Tests

"28 passed, 1468 deselected"

title: PERF: np.isin is very slow for StringDType

labels.name: component: numpy.strings
labels.description: String dtypes and functions

body:
This is more-or-less the same issue as https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/14997 because both object arrays and stringdtype fall back to the `hasobject` path in the `_isin` helper:

https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/30483388e8c07f1abd45b47c534801e9207d2643/numpy/lib/_arraysetops_impl.py#L910-L926

This slow path is much much slower than the sorting path. You can see the difference in this script:

```python
import numpy as np, timeit
a = np.array(['abcd'*5, 'defg'*5, 'abhoj'*6] * 10**4, dtype='T')
print('T:', timeit.timeit(lambda: np.isin(a, a), number=1), 's')
print('U:', timeit.timeit(lambda: np.isin(a.astype('U30'), a.astype('U30')), number=1), 's')
```

On my laptop, this outputs

```
T: 2.9416205829475075 s
U: 0.020494583994150162 s
```

So `StringDType` is orders-of-magnitude slower.

I think an easy fix for this that would help out `StringDType` arrays is to change the predicate in `_is_in` to allow stringdtype to use the sorting path if it has no `na_object` or `na_object` is a string. For nan-like or None-like missing data, we'd need to fall back to the slow object array path.

We could also take the idea from https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/14997 and implement a hash-based `isin` for stringdtype that uses the existing hash-based unique infrastructure. I don't think we can do this for object arrays, but we could maybe allow them to opt in somehow via a keyword argument?

@ikrommyd btw this is sounding very similar to #31969 and is maybe another place we could use HyperLogLog to switch between sorting and hashing to determine set membership with an optimal choice for the dataset's estimated cardinality.

body:
### PR summary
Fixes #32161. Supersedes #32217.

This follows up on recent improvements to StringDType (in particular #32563 and #32464) to enable substantial performance improvements for `isin`. Also adds more tests for `isin` in the `StringDType` tests.

Tests and benchmarks ran on an M1 MacBook Air using Python 3.14. The `pandas.NA` case uses pandas 3.0.5.

| Missing sentinel | Before (`main`) | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| No sentinel | 5.8702 s | 6.923 ms | 848× |
| `None` | 12.6482 s | 5.752 ms | 2,199× |
| `np.nan` | 3.8978 s | 5.636 ms | 692× |
| `"NA"` | 8.3059 s | 6.129 ms | 1,355× |
| `object()` | 12.7385 s | 5.876 ms | 2,168× |
| `pandas.NA` | Raises a casting error | 5.919 ms | — |

For `pandas.NA`, the patch also fixes an error and correctly reports missing entries as non-matches. All returned results were checked against the expected membership mask.

Each baseline was measured once; patched timings are the best of three runs. Input creation is excluded from the timings. Reproduce with `repeats=1` on the baseline and `repeats=3` on the patched build:

```python
import timeit
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

repeats = 3
sentinels = (None, np.nan, "NA", object(), pd.NA)
dtypes = [np.dtypes.StringDType()]
dtypes += [np.dtypes.StringDType(na_object=na) for na in sentinels]
for dtype in dtypes:
    values = ["abcd" * 5, "defg" * 5, "abhoj" * 6]
    if hasattr(dtype, "na_object"):
        values[-1] = dtype.na_object
    a = np.array(values * 10_000, dtype=dtype)
    print(dtype, min(timeit.repeat(lambda: np.isin(a, a),
                                  number=1, repeat=repeats)))
```

body:
### **PR Description**

This PR extends `numpy.ptp` (peak-to-peak: max - min) to support the `where=` keyword argument, consistent with other NumPy reduction functions such as `sum`, `min`, and `max`.

#### **Changes Made**

* Updated `_methods._ptp` to forward `where` into `umr_maximum` and `umr_minimum`.
* Extended public API in `fromnumeric.py` to accept `where=np._NoValue`.
* Updated docstrings to document the new `where` parameter.
* Updated type hints in `fromnumeric.pyi` to include `where`.
* Added unit tests in `test_numeric.py` (`test_ptp_where`) to validate functionality.

#### **Behavior**

* `np.ptp` now honors masks passed via `where`, enabling selective element inclusion in peak-to-peak computation.
* For example:

  ```python
  >>> import numpy as np
  >>> a = np.array([1, 5, 7, 0])
  >>> where = [True, False, True, False]
  >>> np.ptp(a, where=where)
  6
  ```
* Edge cases (e.g., all-False masks) follow the identity rules of `maximum` (`-inf`) and `minimum` (`+inf`), resulting in `-inf` for floating-point arrays.

#### **Testing**

* Added direct test for masked computation.
* Verified broadcasting behavior and compatibility with existing parameters (`axis`, `out`, `keepdims`).

#### **Documentation**

* Added `where` parameter description to the `ptp` docstring.
* `versionadded` tag should be included to mark this feature.

---

This aligns `ptp` with other NumPy reductions and improves API consistency.

---
Fix #29675

title: MAINT: Improve performance of polynomial operations (2)
body:
For many polynomial operations (e.g. add, multiply, negate) the operation takes place on the coefficients of the operands and then a new `Polynomial` is created. For the creation of the new `Polynomial` we can skip the validation of input arguments, as they are either passed from the operands (which have already been validated) or constructed with internal methods (which have validated output).

Benchmark results:
```
p + q: Mean +- std dev: [main0] 31.5 us +- 2.1 us -> [prx] 17.4 us +- 0.6 us: 1.81x faster
p * q: Mean +- std dev: [main0] 32.4 us +- 1.3 us -> [prx] 18.3 us +- 1.0 us: 1.77x faster
2 * p: Mean +- std dev: [main0] 24.3 us +- 1.3 us -> [prx] 11.7 us +- 0.4 us: 2.08x faster
-p: Mean +- std dev: [main0] 14.6 us +- 0.6 us -> [prx] 2.50 us +- 0.11 us: 5.84x faster

Geometric mean: 2.50x faster
```
with script:
```
import pyperf
from numpy.polynomial import Polynomial

setup = """
from numpy.polynomial import Polynomial

p=Polynomial([.5,4,5])
q=Polynomial([1,0,5])
"""

runner = pyperf.Runner()
runner.timeit(name=f"p + q", stmt="_ = p + q", setup=setup)
runner.timeit(name=f"p * q", stmt="_ = p * q", setup=setup)
runner.timeit(name=f"2 * p", stmt="_ = 2 * q", setup=setup)
runner.timeit(name=f"-p", stmt="_ = - p", setup=setup)
```
Notes:

* The `as_series` and `ABCPolyBase.__init__` have an additional flag `_validate_input`. The default is `True` (so the PR is backwards compatible), but for internal operations we set it to `False`
* Testing was performed by with https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/24499 included in both main and the PR. Without https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/24499 there is still a significant performance gain
* We can do even more optimization if we refactor the `polyadd` and/or `polyutils._add` to have a `_validate_input` flag as well. But this requires more refactoring and the `polyadd` is public, so this has not yet been done.
*  The modifications have been made for `__add__`, `__neg__`, `__mul__` and `__rmul__`. If this PR is considered a merge candidate, we can modify other operations as well.

title: ENH: Detect mixed bytes/text inputs during array conversion
body:
### Proposed new feature or change:

Follow-up to [Sebastian’s review comment on #32757](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/32757#discussion_r4080384959).

NumPy currently infers Unicode for mixed bytes/text inputs:

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> np.asarray([b"a", "b"])
array(['a', 'b'], dtype='<U1')
>>> np.concatenate(([b"a", "b"], ["c"]))
array(['a', 'b', 'c'], dtype='<U1')
```

We should add an opt-in mode (exposed to NumPy Python internals via `_array_converter`) that detects these mixtures during dtype discovery, before coercion happens and we lose track of the input dtypes. Shared C conversion machinery would let `concatenate` detect mixtures within its inputs as well as between them.

The same detection could support deprecating implicit Unicode inference for mixed bytes/text inputs. These should eventually produce object arrays that preserve the original values. Explicit conversions such as `dtype="U"` would remain supported.

This has come up in the past, in particular:

- [#15327](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/15327) proposed deprecating implicit string/non-string promotion, including in `concatenate`.
- [#19078](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/19078) described downstream difficulties with promotion warnings: callers wanted numeric inference for numeric inputs and object arrays for mixed inputs.
- [#19101](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/19101) explored an opt-in object-fallback mode during dtype discovery; it was not merged.

title: DEP: Disallow `np.promote_types(string, other) -> string`
body:
It appears that `np.nan` gets converted to the string `"nan"` when initializing an array.

### Reproducing code example:

```python
import numpy as np
np.array(["some string", np.nan])
```
prints
```
array(['some string', 'nan'], dtype='<U11')
```

Similar behavior can be observed for other generators, such as `hstack`, `concat`, `repeat` and `tile`.

### Expected behavior

I would expect that the above returns
```
array(['some string', nan], dtype='object')
```
with the second element of the array being the object `np.nan`.

### Numpy/Python version information:

1.18.1 3.8.2

Under Python 3.11, though for some reason I haven't investigated _not_ 3.10,

```python
import numpy.testing
```

triggers the following `EncodingWarning`
```
$ python -X warn_default_encoding demo.py
numpy/testing/_private/utils.py:1251: EncodingWarning: 'encoding' argument not specified.
  output = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True)
```

title: DEP: deprecate implicit bytes to string conversion in np.strings

labels.name: component: numpy.strings
labels.description: String dtypes and functions

body:
### PR summary
Over in https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/32749/changes#r4072990536 @jorenham and I identified an inconsistency with how python handles mixed string and bytes operands in string and bytes methods.

First, this changes a number of default arguments in `np.strings` from empty string to `None`. This allows us to properly handle bytes operands for these functions and also avoid emitting warnings when the argument is not explicitly passed. To avoid breaking possible downstream `__array_function__` implementations, I only pass these arguments if a user sets them, so downstream can continue assuming the argument is always a string.

Second, it deprecates calls like `np.strings.replace(b"abc", "a", "x")` that silently mix text and bytes. This is deprecated for `replace`, `partition`, and text-padding functions. My AI model found concrete downstream sites in where this pattern happens:

- [AtomWorks](https://github.com/RosettaCommons/atomworks/blob/fcf7af8c127e0de62a460dab5230c649a25a78d4/src/atomworks/ml/transforms/af3_reference_molecule.py#L134): casts atom names to `S4`, then calls `np.char.ljust(..., fillchar=" ")`.
- [NVIDIA Proteina-Complexa](https://github.com/NVIDIA-BioNeMo/Proteina-Complexa/blob/33b76585801eb902802cc7410c85bc37ae81b346/src/proteinfoundation/datasets/atomworks_ligand_transforms.py#L47): the same padding pattern.
- [ugali](https://github.com/DarkEnergySurvey/ugali/blob/0ef58e8c95617d8be0db18916cc6c368e8e2b298/ugali/analysis/search.py#L454): calls `np.char.replace(objects['NAME'], '_', ' ')` on an `S24` field.

It also adds machinery in `_array_converter` to facilitate these checks.

Finally, updates the type stubs to match these changes.

#### AI Disclosure
I iterated on this using an AI model.

title: ENH: support N-D arrays in `np.searchsorted ` by searching along the last axis
body:
### PR summary
Closes #4224.

`np.searchsorted` and `ndarray.searchsorted` no longer require the sorted array to be one-dimensional. Each 1-D slice along the last axis is searched independently. There is no `axis` keyword: to search along another axis, bring it to the end first, for instance with `np.moveaxis`.

Internally this is four private gufuncs, `_searchsorted_{left,right}` with signature `(n),(m?)->(m?)` and `_searchsorted_{left,right}_sorter` with `(n),(m?),(n)->(m?)`. `side` picks the gufunc statically, so the kernels in `npysort/binsearch.cpp` are unchanged and still selected as `get_binsearch_func(dtype, side)` did.

`(n),(m?)->(m?)` is the signature and what array-api-extra implements, with the flexible `m?` so a scalar `v` keeps returning a scalar. Keys are `v`'s last axis and leading axes broadcast against `a`'s other dimensions. The searched dimension of the result lands last, which is the plain gufunc default, so no `axes` juggling is needed and the layout matches JAX and array-api-extra. Regarding Jake's question, there is no `batch_dims` equivalent, leading dims broadcast right-aligned, so the batched cases need a `newaxis` manually from the user. Against array-api-extra the results agree wherever both accept a call, and numpy additionally broadcasts in both directions, takes a `sorter`, promotes `a` and `v` by value, and covers every dtype with a comparison rather than real numbers only.

The gufunc is an internal layer rather than the Python entry point: dispatch stays in C, `PyArray_SearchSorted` is unchanged and serves as the fallback, and the legacy `ArrFunc_Compare` layer is untouched. The dtype slot is not here, but a registered loop is the only thing that grants a dtype N-D support, which is the seam a `searchsorted_meth` slot plugs into, so that follow-up is additive and would close the existing `TODO` in `item_selection.c`. Exposing `axis` later is additive in the same way.

N-D works for all builtin dtypes and for run-time registered ones via a promoter. StringDType stays 1-D for now and says so, rather than only reporting the depth of `a`.

#### AI Disclosure
AI has been used a lot in brainstorming about this PR about the signature and potential ways to implement the PR and to create quick rough sketches to try out myself which would have taken me many days to do manually. Eventually I iterated with AI to figure out how to logically do the dtype handling and for review.

body: ### PR Summary This PR does two things 1) fixes dtype mismatch in `c-info.python-as-glue.rst` Currently, in the cython zadd function snippet, ```python cdef double complex[:] a = in1.ravel() cdef double complex[:] b = in2.ravel() out = np.empty(a.shape[0], np.complex64) cdef double complex[:] c = out.ravel() ``` the `out` dtype is `np.complex64`. However, the very nextline slices `double complex` which is `np.complex128` . This, when compiled and run, gives following `ValueError`. Fix : Simply change `out` dtype to `np.complex128` to match it. This works fine and adds two complex numbers. (Here, `main.py` imports `zadd` function from compiled cython file, and adds two complex128). 2) improves an example snippet in `basics.types.rst` It says > Sometimes the conversion can overflow, for instance when converting a `numpy.int64` value 300 to `numpy.int8`. NumPy follows C casting rules, so that value would overflow and become 44 ``(300 - 256)``. If you wish to avoid such overflows, you can specify that the overflow action fail by using ``same_value`` for the ``casting`` argument (see also :ref:`overflow-errors`):: Currently, the example for type casting, which aimed to demomstrate ValueError when type casting with `casting='same_value'` option, shows ``` >>> z.astype(np.float64, casting="same_value") array([0., 1., 2.]) ``` Here z is array `[0, 1, 2]`. This example failed to emphasize the said actual behaviour Hence, it can be replaced with following example ``` >>> w = np.array([126,127,128],dtype=np.int64) >>> w.astype(np.int8, casting='same_value') Traceback (most recent call last): File "", line 1, in ValueError: could not cast 'same_value' long to byte ``` I ran `spin docs` and verified both the changes in built html document. #### AI Disclosure Claude Code assisted me in finding these bugs.

title: SubTracker: Convert static types (PyTypeObject) to heap types via `PyType_FromModuleAndSpec`
body:
Part of https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/32451 and https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/31913. This is intended to be a tracking issue for a series of PRs converting NumPy's static types to heap types.

NumPy currently defines its types (`ndarray`, `dtype`, `ufunc`, scalars, iterators, etc.) as static `PyTypeObject`s. Static types are shared by every interpreter in the process, including their `tp_dict` and reference counts, so they can't be isolated per interpreter. The CPython [Isolating Extension Modules](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/isolating-extensions.html#heap-types) guide recommends replacing them with heap types created by [`PyType_FromModuleAndSpec`](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/type.html#c.PyType_FromModuleAndSpec).

This issue depends on multi-phase init (#29021) and generally follows the [Changing Static Types to Heap Types](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/isolating-extensions.html#changing-static-types-to-heap-types) section of the guide:

Converting to heap types is also a prerequisite for building against the [Limited API](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/stable.html#limited-c-api), where static `PyTypeObject` definitions are not possible, see  https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/31913.

title: BUG: `from_dlpack` runs the capsule destructor with a pending exception → spurious `SystemError` and skipped producer deleter

labels.name: 57 - Close?
labels.description: Issues which may be closable unless discussion continued

body:
### Describe the issue:

**Versions**: numpy 2.5.2, Python 3.12.14, Linux x86_64 (cp312 wheel)

## Summary

`np.from_dlpack` raises `SystemError: <built-in function from_dlpack> returned NULL
without setting an exception` (a CPython C-API violation) — instead of the intended
`BufferError: Unsupported dtype in DLTensor.` — when the incoming DLPack tensor has a
dtype that numpy does not support (e.g. `kDLOpaqueHandle` code=3, bfloat code=4, or a
known code with unsupported bits). On top of masking the error, the producer's capsule
deleter (its free hook) is never invoked, so the `DLManagedTensor` and the managed buffer
are leaked.

The root cause is that the error path DECREFs the input capsule (running the producer's
destructor, which may be Python code) **while the exception is still set**.

### Reproduce the code example:

```python
import numpy as np, ctypes, gc
from ctypes import (pythonapi, CFUNCTYPE, POINTER, Structure, cast,
                    c_void_p, c_char_p, c_int32, c_int64, c_uint8, c_uint16, c_uint64)

class DLDevice(Structure):    _fields_ = [("device_type", c_int32), ("device_id", c_int32)]
class DLDataType(Structure):  _fields_ = [("code", c_uint8), ("bits", c_uint8), ("lanes", c_uint16)]
class DLTensor(Structure):
    _fields_ = [("data", c_void_p), ("device", DLDevice), ("ndim", c_int32),
                ("dtype", DLDataType), ("shape", POINTER(c_int64)),
                ("strides", POINTER(c_int64)), ("byte_offset", c_uint64)]
DELETER_FN = CFUNCTYPE(None, c_void_p)
class DLManagedTensor(Structure): pass
DLManagedTensor._fields_ = [("dl_tensor", DLTensor), ("manager_ctx", c_void_p), ("deleter", DELETER_FN)]

_PyCapsule_New = pythonapi.PyCapsule_New
_PyCapsule_New.restype = ctypes.py_object
_PyCapsule_New.argtypes = [c_void_p, c_char_p, c_void_p]
_GetPointer = pythonapi.PyCapsule_GetPointer
_GetPointer.restype = c_void_p
_GetPointer.argtypes = [c_void_p, c_char_p]

deleter_calls = {"n": 0}

@DELETER_FN
def deleter(p):
    deleter_calls["n"] += 1            # the producer's free hook

@CFUNCTYPE(None, c_void_p)
def cap_destructor(p):                 # Python-level capsule destructor
    try:
        d = cast(_GetPointer(p, b"dltensor"), POINTER(DLManagedTensor))
        if d.contents.deleter:
            d.contents.deleter(_GetPointer(p, b"dltensor"))
    except Exception:
        pass

_KEEP = []
class Producer:
    def __init__(self, code):
        self.arr = np.arange(4, dtype=np.int32)
        self.code = code
    def __dlpack__(self, *a, **k):     # returns a *fresh* capsule (refcount 1)
        arr = self.arr; n = arr.ndim
        shape = (c_int64 * n)(*arr.shape)
        strides = (c_int64 * n)(*(arr.strides[i] // arr.itemsize for i in range(n)))
        dt = DLTensor(); dt.data = c_void_p(arr.ctypes.data); dt.device = DLDevice(1, 0); dt.ndim = n
        dt.dtype = DLDataType(self.code, 32, 1); dt.shape = shape; dt.strides = strides; dt.byte_offset = 0
        dlmt = DLManagedTensor(); dlmt.dl_tensor = dt; dlmt.manager_ctx = c_void_p(self.code); dlmt.deleter = deleter
        ptr = ctypes.pointer(dlmt); _KEEP.extend([arr, shape, strides, dlmt, ptr])
        return _PyCapsule_New(cast(ptr, c_void_p), b"dltensor", cast(cap_destructor, c_void_p))
    def __dlpack_device__(self):
        return (1, 0)

p = Producer(3)                          # kDLOpaqueHandle — numpy does not support it
try:
    np.from_dlpack(p)
except BaseException as e:
    print(f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}")
del p
for _ in range(4):
    gc.collect()
print("deleter calls:", deleter_calls["n"])
```

### Error message:

```shell
## Expected behavior


BufferError: Unsupported dtype in DLTensor.
deleter calls: 1          # capsule released, producer free hook runs once


(`BufferError` is the documented intent — see PR #31000 and
`dlpack_dtype_registry_lookup()` in `numpy/_core/src/multiarray/dlpack.c`.)

## Actual behavior


SystemError: <built-in function from_dlpack> returned NULL without setting an exception
deleter calls: 0          # deleter never invoked -> DLManagedTensor + buffer leaked


and the following is written to stderr (the smoking gun — the destructor runs with a
pending exception):


Exception ignored on calling ctypes callback function: <function cap_destructor ...>
SystemError: <method 'get' of 'dict' objects> returned a result with an exception set


Other unsupported dtype codes reproduce the same: `code=4` (bfloat), `5`, `7`, `255`, and
a known code with unsupported bits (e.g. `code=kDLInt=0` with `bits=24`) all raise
`SystemError` and skip the deleter.
```

### Python and NumPy Versions:

**Versions**: numpy 2.5.2, Python 3.12.14, Linux x86_64 (cp312 wheel)

### Runtime Environment:

**Versions**: numpy 2.5.2, Python 3.12.14, Linux x86_64 (cp312 wheel)

### How does this issue affect you or how did you find it:

## Why this happens

In `numpy/_core/src/multiarray/dlpack.c`, `from_dlpack()` falls through to the dtype
registry on an unknown dtype code:

```c
    } else {
        descr = dlpack_dtype_registry_lookup((uint8_t)dl_tensor.dtype.code, bits);
        if (descr == NULL) {
            Py_DECREF(capsule);        // <-- runs the producer destructor
            return NULL;               //     while the BufferError below is still set
        }
    }
```

and the helper sets the exception first:

```c
    if (gres == 0) {
        PyErr_SetString(PyExc_BufferError, "Unsupported dtype in DLTensor.");
        return NULL;
    }
```

So `Py_DECREF(capsule)` executes arbitrary producer code (the capsule destructor) while
`BufferError` is pending. For a Python-implemented destructor (ctypes, or any deleter that
acquires the GIL and touches Python objects) the nested Python call collides with the
pending exception, raising `SystemError` inside the destructor. ctypes then clears the
exception state ("Exception ignored ..."), the destructor aborts *before* it can invoke the
producer's deleter, and `from_dlpack` returns NULL with no exception set — which CPython
surfaces as the outer `SystemError`.

This is the classic C-API rule "do not run arbitrary code (which `Py_DECREF` can trigger
via destructors/finalizers) with a pending exception." Note the same `PyErr_SetString(...);
Py_DECREF(capsule); return NULL;` pattern is used by the other error branches (device,
lanes, maxdims) in this function, so they would be affected the same way.

## Why the existing tests don't catch it

`test_dlpack.py::TestDLPack::test_invalid_dtype` uses numpy itself as the *producer*
(`np.from_dlpack(x)` where `x` is an ndarray), so the capsule destructor is numpy's own C
deleter (`array_dlpack_deleter`), which does not run Python-level code — hence no
`SystemError` and the test passes. A foreign, Python-implemented producer (the standard way
to build a DLPack capsule in tests, e.g. in IREE/TensorFlow) is what exercises this path.

## Diagnostic

Registering the dtype makes the failure disappear, confirming the registry error path is the
trigger:

```python
np.dtypes.register_dlpack_dtype((3, 32), np.dtype("int32"))
np.from_dlpack(Producer(3))   # now succeeds and releases the capsule
np.from_dlpack(Producer(3))   # now succeeds and releases the capsule
```

title: Transition `PyArray_PythonPyIntFromInt` to modern behavior

labels.name: sustain-2026
labels.description: Issues reserved for NumFOCUS Sustaining Open Source Series 2026

body:
`PyArray_PythonPyIntFromInt` existed to not change behavior of existing code that used the `"i"` format in Python.
But along the way, Python fixed their things, the conversion now uses `__index__` as it should and rejects all non-integers (not just floats explictly).

We missed that and while we used to be ahead of the curve we are now behind here.  So what we should do is:
* Try the `__index__` style conversion.  (this is a tiny bug fix as well)
* If that fails, try current code with a warning.

It would be nice to audit if there are remaining `"i"` uses that matters, because if there aren't we can be clearer about when the warning was introduced (i.e. we won't use it for more functions).

Additionally, it may be nice to do a check whether all integers are used in places where NumPy may just want to directly transition to _our_ integer conversion helpers.  These differ in that NumPy sometimes rejects booleans.
(This doesn't matter much either way, the bool rejecting matters mostly in places that are slightly indexing related.)

title: DOC: unicode/str/bytes in Python 3

labels.name: sustain-2026
labels.description: Issues reserved for NumFOCUS Sustaining Open Source Series 2026

body:
### Issue with current documentation:

1. The documentation In [`numpy/core/defchararray.py`](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/main/numpy/core/defchararray.py) still makes a distinction between `str` and `unicode`, for historical reasons I suppose:
https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/8d2ddb53a9dae2d90a752ad4995c30817049fe06/numpy/core/defchararray.py#L6-L13
The code itself, including internal function names, still uses the terms `unicode` and `str`, and as far as I can see always as aliases of `bytes` and `str`. As a first step, without modifying the code itself , shouldn't occurrences of `unicode` be removed from the documentation? Or `unicode` and `str` changed to `str` and `bytes`? I am not sure as I haven't understood yet the expected type of `_vec_string()` arguments.
I suppose "_if the corresponding string method is  available in your version of Python_" refers to Python 2. Shouldn't this sentence be removed?

2. I can still see [`string_`](https://numpy.org/doc/1.21/reference/arrays.scalars.html#numpy.string_) and [`unicode_`](https://numpy.org/doc/1.21/reference/arrays.scalars.html#numpy.unicode_) used in the documentation, but nowadays these are aliases of [`bytes_`](https://numpy.org/doc/1.21/reference/arrays.scalars.html#numpy.bytes_) and [`str_`](https://numpy.org/doc/1.21/reference/arrays.scalars.html#numpy.str_) respectively. Shouldn't all occurrences of [`string_`](https://numpy.org/doc/1.21/reference/arrays.scalars.html#numpy.string_) and [`unicode_`](https://numpy.org/doc/1.21/reference/arrays.scalars.html#numpy.unicode_) be changed to [`bytes_`](https://numpy.org/doc/1.21/reference/arrays.scalars.html#numpy.bytes_) and [`str_`](https://numpy.org/doc/1.21/reference/arrays.scalars.html#numpy.str_)?

3. Then perhaps the code itself in [`numpy/core/defchararray.py`](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/main/numpy/core/defchararray.py) should be changed accordingly.

4. Shouldn't the `unicode` keyword argument disappear? For example:
    `class numpy.chararray(shape, itemsize=1, unicode=False, buffer=None, offset=0, strides=None, order=None)`
 
5. Finally:
https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/8d2ddb53a9dae2d90a752ad4995c30817049fe06/numpy/core/defchararray.py#L15
Yet the documentation has two duplicate entries. Shouldn't the second entry point to the first one?
   * [`numpy.chararray`](https://numpy.org/doc/1.21/reference/generated/numpy.chararray.html)
   * [`numpy.char.chararray`](https://numpy.org/doc/1.21/reference/generated/numpy.char.chararray.html)

title: BUG: floor timedelta64 // int for negative values
body:
### PR summary

`timedelta64 // int` was wired to the same loop as true division (`TIMEDELTA_mq_m_divide`), which uses C truncating `/`. For negative values that means rounding toward zero, while `int64 // int`, `timedelta64 // timedelta64`, and Python `datetime.timedelta // int` all floor.

This adds a real `TIMEDELTA_mq_m_floor_divide` loop (including the existing SIMD floor path with NaT propagation for the `mQ->m` result) and stops aliasing `floor_divide` `mq` to `divide`. True division `timedelta64 / int` is unchanged and still truncates.

Closes #32522

### First time committer introduction

I use NumPy in day to day Python work and was looking for a small, well scoped correctness bug to contribute. Issue #32522 is a clear ufunc contract mismatch with a focused fix path, so I worked through the timedelta division loops and tests there.

#### AI Disclosure

Cursor (Composer agent) was used to help locate the `mq` floor_divide alias in `generate_umath.py` / `loops_arithmetic_timedelta.dispatch.cpp`, draft the `TIMEDELTA_mq_m_floor_divide` implementation and tests, build locally on Windows, and open this PR. I reviewed the change, checked it against the issue reproduction and related floor vs trunc cases, and am responsible for the submitted code and this description.

```py
def double(x: float) -> float: ...
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int: ...

u = np.frompyfunc(double, 1, 1)
v = np.frompyfunc(add, 2, 1)

reveal_type(u(np.ones((2, 3))))
# before: float | NDArray[object_[Any]]
# after:  ndarray[tuple[int, int], dtype[object_[float]]]

reveal_type(v(np.arange(3), 1))
# before: int | NDArray[object_[Any]]
# after:  ndarray[tuple[int], dtype[object_[int]]]

reveal_type(v.reduce([1, 2, 3]))
# before: int | NDArray[object_[Any]]
# after:  int
```

title: TYP: ``poly1d`` shape-typing
body:
The array types of `np.poly1d` are now narrowed to have 1d shape-type, because suprisingly, `poly1d` is 1d. There's one exception though, and that's when 0d or >1d array-likes are passed as `val` to `np.poly1d.__call__`, in which case the shape is preserved. So this also adds overloads to `__call__` so that arrays with known shape-type return an exact shape-type, and bare scalar-likes, 1d- and 2d array-like sequences also return a rank-2 array. 

I've used `Incomplete` instead of `Any` for scalar-types (which `Incomplete`  simply aliases) because it's possible, and even feasible, to make those exact. Doing so would require turning `poly1d` into a generic type though, so that's out of scope here, and probably needs to be discussed a bit to see if we actually want to do that (seeing as `poly1d` is considered legacy-ish functionality). So I guess I'll put it on the agenda for tomorrow's community meeting.

---

Pair programmed with AI.

title: TYP: ``vectorize`` shape-typing
body:
`np.vectorize` now has shape-typing support, and has been made aware of the arity and return type of the vectorized user function. 
It was a bit tricky to get this right because `vectorize` can both be used as a decorator and directly, and then there's also the `signature` which influences the output. After hammering at it to get it as simple as feasible, I'm pretty happy with how it turned out.

```py
import numpy as np

def relu(x: float) -> float:
    return max(x, 0.0)

image = np.ones((2, 3))

reveal_type(np.vectorize(relu)(image))
# before: Any
# after:  ndarray[tuple[int, int], dtype[float64]]

reveal_type(np.vectorize(str)(np.arange(3)))
# before: Any
# after:  ndarray[tuple[int], dtype[str_]]
```

title: PERF: avoid temporary boolean array in np.array_equal for contiguous integer arrays

labels.name: triage review
labels.description: Issue/PR to be discussed at the next triage meeting

body:
### Proposed new feature or change

`np.array_equal()` currently implements its normal comparison path as:

```python
builtins.bool((asanyarray(a1 == a2)).all())
```

This materializes an elementwise boolean array and then reduces it in a second pass. For same-shape, same-dtype, contiguous arrays of NumPy's built-in signed/unsigned integer dtypes, equality can instead be fused, potentially with a bytewise comparison. This would avoid the temporary allocation and allow an early exit on mismatches.

A conservative fast path would require both converted operands to be exact ndarrays, equal shapes and identical built-in signed/unsigned integer dtypes, and the same contiguous traversal order (both C-contiguous or both F-contiguous). Unsupported cases would retain the current implementation.

A raw-byte path should **not** initially include `bool` (distinct nonzero bytes can both mean true), floating-point (for example, `0.0 == -0.0`), object, structured, flexible, or user-defined dtypes. For built-in integers, `equal_nan` does not affect the result.

Conceptually:

```c
if (same_builtin_integer_dtype &&
        same_shape &&
        compatible_contiguous_layout) {
    return memcmp(data1, data2, nbytes) == 0;
}
```

The implementation need not literally use `memcmp`; a NumPy SIMD-aware fused compare/early-exit helper may be preferable. An identity check can also make `np.array_equal(a, a)` constant-time for these dtypes.

### Prototype benchmark

I tested a narrow C prototype on NumPy main commit `d2cf21758a32029b4c614fc90c2fc5dcbcf07a9c` (2026-08-31). The helper uses `memcmp` only for identical built-in integer dtypes and compatible C/F-contiguous layouts, and otherwise returns `NotImplemented` to the existing path.

Following the benchmark style used in recent NumPy performance PRs, I added parameterized ASV `time_` benchmarks with setup outside the timed method and ran:

```console
cd benchmarks
asv continuous d2cf21758a32029b4c614fc90c2fc5dcbcf07a9c HEAD \
    -b "bench_array_equal" --interleave-rounds --show-stderr
```

Machine: AMD Ryzen 5 3400G, Linux x86-64, Python 3.12.

| case | current main | prototype | ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 10M int64, equal, C | 7.49 ms | 5.67 ms | 0.76 |
| 10M int64, mismatch in middle, C | 7.30 ms | 2.90 ms | 0.40 |
| 10M int64, mismatch first, C | 6.93 ms | 11.9 µs | 0.0017 |
| 10M int64, mismatch last, C | 7.56 ms | 5.61 ms | 0.74 |
| 10M int8, equal, C | 2.21 ms | 785 µs | 0.36 |
| 10M int8, mismatch first, C | 1.51 ms | 9.74 µs | 0.0065 |
| 10M int8, mismatch in middle, C | 1.92 ms | 399 µs | 0.21 |
| 10M int8, mismatch last, C | 2.23 ms | 790 µs | 0.35 |

F-contiguous results were similar. At one million elements, all eight built-in signed/unsigned integer dtypes improved. For first-element mismatches:

| dtype | current main | prototype |
|---|---:|---:|
| int8 | 63.0 µs | 4.75 µs |
| uint8 | 64.8 µs | 4.71 µs |
| int16 | 274 µs | 7.65 µs |
| uint16 | 267 µs | 7.44 µs |
| int32 | 546 µs | 8.56 µs |
| uint32 | 567 µs | 9.64 µs |
| int64 | 708 µs | 9.78 µs |
| uint64 | 713 µs | 10.5 µs |

Short contiguous integer arrays (10 and 1,000 elements) did not regress in this run. Explicit fallback controls also showed no measured regression:

| unsupported path | current main | prototype |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1M float64, equal | 871 µs | 824 µs |
| 1M bool, equal | 107 µs | 90.2 µs |
| 1M strided int64, equal | 1.48 ms | 1.45 ms |

Those small fallback differences should be treated as noise; the important result is that the added dispatch was not measurably slower.

The core ASV benchmark shape was:

```python
class ArrayEqualContiguousInteger:
    params = [
        [10, 1_000, 10_000_000],
        ["int8", "int64"],
        ["equal", "early", "middle", "late"],
        ["C", "F"],
    ]
    param_names = ["size", "dtype", "difference", "order"]

    def setup(self, size, dtype, difference, order):
        shape = (size // 10, 10)
        self.a = np.arange(size, dtype=dtype).reshape(shape, order=order)
        self.b = self.a.copy(order=order)
        if difference != "equal":
            index = {
                "early": 0,
                "middle": size // 2,
                "late": size - 1,
            }[difference]
            self.b.ravel(order=order)[index] ^= 1

    def time_array_equal(self, size, dtype, difference, order):
        np.array_equal(self.a, self.b)
```

### Temporary memory

I also measured process peak RSS in fresh subprocesses after constructing two 10M-element `int64` arrays. The current `(a == b).all()` path increased peak RSS by 9,816 KiB; the prototype increased it by 0 KiB. The result was the same for equal arrays and a first-element mismatch. This is consistent with eliminating the 10M-byte boolean temporary.

### Correctness checks

The prototype passed focused checks for all eight integer dtypes, C- and F-contiguous multidimensional arrays, equal and unequal values, identity, empty arrays, and `equal_nan=True`. Tests also verified that bool (including distinct nonzero true representations), float, mixed byte order, mixed dtype, and strided arrays use the existing fallback.

### Scope

This issue proposes only the built-in contiguous integer case. If a fused equality primitive proves maintainable, dtype-specific loops could later cover strided integers, floating-point semantics, or other fixed-width dtypes.

I had to revert to using legacy `TypeVar`'s because it turns out that Pyright has a bug in it's "variance" (which is actually called "polarity" in the literature) inference algorithm, causing Pyright to incorrectly infer the generic scalar-type and shape-type parameters as invariant rather than covariant (`NamedTuple` is immutable, `dtype` is covariant in scalar-type, and `ndarray` is covariant in shape-type, so it should be covariant here as well).
The corresponding type-tests for these functions, as well as those for `np.unique_counts`, are now also more representative of real-world usage (instead of asserting against a nominal private-API named tuple type with type-check-only generic params).

title: BUG: make void scalar ellipsis indexing consistent
body:
### PR summary

Closes #32742.

`voidtype_subscript` had special casing only for the single ellipsis before running every other index through `PyArray_Return`  which made `v[...,]` get demoted back to `np.void` while `v[...]` returned a 0d array.
We scope `PyArray_Return` to field selection so that every other index behaves as it does on the equivalent 0d array.
This felt more natural as other scalar types have no special casing and let `array_subscript` decide the return type.
If you'd rather have another if statement for the 1-element ellipsis tuple, let me know.

Of course this has implications on `np.record` which just forwards  indexing to `np.void` so the following
```
In [1]: r = np.rec.array([(1, 2.0)], dtype=[('x', 'i4'), ('y', 'f8')])[0]

In [2]: r
Out[2]: np.record((1, 2.0), dtype=[('x', '<i4'), ('y', '<f8')])

In [3]: r[...]
Out[3]: array((1, 2.), dtype=(numpy.record, [('x', '<i4'), ('y', '<f8')]))

In [4]: r[...,]
Out[4]: np.record((1, 2.0), dtype=[('x', '<i4'), ('y', '<f8')])
```
returns an array in both cases on the PR branch. But this is what it should do IMO.

If there is a reason to have the 1-element ellipsis tuple behave differently, we can just close this and the issue.

AI wrote the test cause I was lazy

title: BUG: Indexing a void array scalar with `(...,)` does not return an `ndarray`
body:
### Describe the issue:

Admittedly I have not found any documentation that explicitly states what indexing with `(...,)` should do, but I did find: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/48fecee5453aa1d31e6b79dcb3969dc1a6d1a891/doc/source/reference/arrays.scalars.rst#L461-L465
from which it can be deduced that `x[y]` should produce the same output as `x[...][y]` for any `y`, including `y=(...,)`. This is indeed how it works with e.g. `np.float64`:
```
>>> import numpy as np
>>> x = np.float64(0)
>>> x[(...,)]
array(0.)
>>> x[...][(...,)]
array(0.)
```
but it is not how it works with void array scalars:
```
>>> v = np.void(3, dtype=[("x", np.int8)])
>>> v[(...,)]
np.void((3,), dtype=[('x', 'i1')])
>>> v[...][(...,)]
array((3,), dtype=[('x', 'i1')])
```
Furthermore, when running mypy on the code example below it reports
```
demo.py:7: note: Revealed type is "numpy.ndarray[tuple[()], numpy.dtype[numpy.void]]"
Success: no issues found in 1 source file
```
so the current runtime behavior is inconsistent with type annotations.

### Reproduce the code example:

```python
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

import numpy as np

v = np.void(3, dtype=[("x", np.int8)])
if TYPE_CHECKING:
    reveal_type(v[(...,)])
assert isinstance(v[(...,)], np.ndarray)
```

### Error message:

```shell
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../demo.py", line 8, in <module>
    assert isinstance(v[(...,)], np.ndarray), type[v[(...,)]]
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AssertionError: type[np.void((3, 3), dtype=[('x', 'i1')])]
```

### Python and NumPy Versions:

2.5.2
3.12.3 (main, Aug 31 2026, 10:18:26) [GCC 13.3.0]

### Runtime Environment:

_No response_

### How does this issue affect you or how did you find it:

I was working on adding type annotations to a library that uses custom dtypes, and I discovered that I could make the annotations consistent with numpy annotations or with runtime behavior but not both.

title: DEP: Deprecate `dot` for with more than 2 dimensions

labels.name: sustain-2026
labels.description: Issues reserved for NumFOCUS Sustaining Open Source Series 2026

body:
`np.dot()` and `arr.dot()` have a fun "dimension-interleaving" behavior for more than two dimensions.
In practice, this actually only matters when the second array has more than 2 dimensions (and the first more than one).

In that case, `dot` behaves like `tensordot(..., axes=[-1, -2])` and the result shape is something like `a.shape + b.shape "- axes"`.

This seems confusing and for most cases `tensordot` should be faster anyway because it lowers to BLAS (but may copy for reshaping) or `@/matmul` would be clearer (because it does outer broadcasting).

We should slowly deprecate the confusing paths or all >2D inputs. Probably deprecting all `>2D` because otherwise we need to add reshape or "use matmul" logic to get BLAS acceleration.

(This is related to/a follow up from gh-31575)

title: DOC: signature of `__array__`

labels.name: sustain-2026
labels.description: Issues reserved for NumFOCUS Sustaining Open Source Series 2026

body:
### Issue with current documentation:

On https://numpy.org/devdocs/user/basics.interoperability.html#dunder-array-interface it is stated that the signature of `__array__` should be `__array__(self, dtype=None, copy=None)`, i.e. arguments are either positional or keyword-based.
However, `numpy.ndarray.__array__` has `__array__([dtype, ]*, copy=None)`, i.e. with keyword-only `copy`, see https://numpy.org/devdocs/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.__array__.html#numpy.ndarray.__array__

This means that `np.array(a,int,True)` works for a user-defined `a` that follows the documentation but not for `numpy.ndarray`.

Note that this was mentioned in https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/30873, but I understand the `nonfix` as related to the typing issue.

### Idea or request for content:

There are two options:
1. Change the implementation of `numpy.ndarray.__array__`: Not a DOC change and enforcing a keyword argument was probably a conscious decision for reasons unknown to me.
2. Update the documentation and suggest a to have the same signature as `numpy.ndarray.__array__`.

All code where the `copy` argument is given via a keyword will continue to work in both cases.

title: Tracking Issue: Support for CPython subinterpreters in NumPy
body:
**Description:**
This issue tracks the architectural changes required to support [CPython subinterpreters](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/subinterpreters.html), to safely support multiple interpreters running simultaneously, NumPy must stop relying on global shared memory and ensure every interpreter gets its own distinct module instance.

**Initial Roadmap:**
Following CPython's [Isolating Extension Modules](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/isolating-extensions.html#isolating-extensions-howto) guide, we will start with:

* #29021 (This is an already on going effort by @AA-Turner)
* #31930
* #32747 

**Expected Outcomes for this phase:**
* Core modules can be safely imported multiple times across different subinterpreters without memory leaks or race conditions.

Other references:  https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/24755
